messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Kwame is a forty-six-year-old park ranger who has spent the last fifteen years patrolling the remote trails and campgrounds of a national forest in the Pacific Northwest. He came to therapy at the urging of his supervisor after an incident three weeks ago: a firefighting helicopter flew low over his patrol area, and Kwame froze mid-step on the trail, his vision narrowing until he could see only the sky, the thud of rotors pressing into his chest. A hiker found him standing motionless, unresponsive, for nearly five minutes. When he came back to himself he was drenched in sweat, the smell of jet fuel and something metallic clinging to his memory. He had not felt that detached and unreal since his deployment, and the experience terrified him more than the helicopter itself.

The event that first taught Kwame to fear the sound of rotors happened twenty years ago in Somalia, during a peacekeeping mission gone wrong. He was a combat medic assigned to a supply convoy that came under ambush in a narrow alley. His squad leader called for a medevac, and Kwame remembers watching the Black Hawk descend through a haze of smoke and dust. He remembers the smell: hot oil, cordite, and the coppery weight of blood soaking into the sand. The helicopter took a rocket-propelled grenade just as it touched down, and within seconds the aircraft was a burning skeleton. Kwame pulled two men from the wreckage, but three others died. For years afterward he has told himself what he already knows: there was nothing more he could have done. The helicopter was hit before he could get close. Yet the guilt sits inside him like a stone, unshiftable. He will never forgive himself for not stopping it—for not somehow preventing the ambush, for not dragging the others out faster. He believes the event permanently damaged him, that something essential in his personality broke that day and never healed. He came home from Somalia and tried to resume civilian life, but he was certain he had become a different person: someone who could not relax, who had to be on guard all the time.

As a park ranger, Kwame had hoped the quiet of the woods would settle his nerves. For a while it worked. He could walk miles without seeing another person, and the silence felt like a reprieve. But the helicopters kept finding him. Fire season brought water-dropping aircraft skimming the ridgelines. Search-and-rescue flights crossed his sector twice a month. Every time the thumping started in the distance, Kwame’s body reacted before his mind caught up: his shoulders tensed, his breathing quickened, and he began scanning the tree line for signs of threat. He watched hikers closely, studying their hands, their backpacks, the set of their jaws—looking for the flicker of intention that might precede an attack. He had come to believe that danger could appear anywhere, at any moment, and that he was the only one who could detect it. When unexpected sounds happened—a branch snapping, a vehicle backfiring, a child shouting—his entire nervous system snapped to attention. He had to be ready.

The memories themselves did not fade. They stayed vivid, as clear as live video inside his head. He could replay the ambush second by second. What unsettled him most was the olfactory recall: sometimes, for no evident reason, he would catch the smell of the burning helicopter—a mix of fuel, melted wiring, and singed fabric—as though it were in the room with him. Those moments made his stomach turn and his vision swim, and he would reach out to steady himself against a tree, feeling the ordinary world slip into something less real. Ordinary memories felt thin and grey by comparison. Only the combat memory had weight and texture.

Over the years, Kwame’s avoidance had become a quiet but steady erosion of his life. He stopped attending his wife’s family gatherings because too many people meant too many faces to watch. He volunteered for the most isolated patrols, staying overnight in backcountry cabins so he would not have to sit in the ranger station where radios sometimes squawked with aviation traffic. His wife told him he had become a stranger, always watching the horizon, never fully present at the dinner table. She did not know about the flashback smells—he had never described them to anyone—but she knew that the man she married had grown wary and withdrawn. Kwame knew he had changed for the worse. He felt hollowed out by the hypervigilance, exhausted by the constant policing of his environment. There was no part of his daily life that felt safe.

What finally brought him to the clinic was not the guilt or the memories. It was the episode on the trail, the moment he went blank in front of a stranger. His supervisor told him he could not return to full duty without a psychological evaluation, and the threat of losing his job—the last place where he felt even remotely competent—pushed him through the door. In his first session, Kwame sat forward in the chair, hands clasped, and said he wanted two things: to stop freezing when he heard a helicopter, and to be able to look at his wife without feeling like he was hiding something. He did not mention forgiveness. He did not think he deserved it. But he wanted the grip of the past to loosen, even a little, so he could walk through his park without feeling like he was still in that alley, waiting for a bird of fire to fall from the sky.
